note: The bundled SearXNG. Two switches gate a search and BOTH are needed: each persona carries its own web_search flag (it travels in the .pyr), and this registration is the workspace's egress control, which a bundle deliberately cannot carry -- what a tenant may call out to is not the bundle author's decision. No max_calls_per_session: research is not rationed here. The engines are named because it decides whether this sample works at all. The big WEB engines refuse an ordinary self-hosted address (duckduckgo serves a CAPTCHA; brave, startpage, qwant and yahoo block), and a refused search returns HTTP 200 with zero results -- indistinguishable from a model that chose not to search. Their NEWS siblings are different engines and answer fine. That distinction is the whole game for a daily paper: measured here, the general set ranks by relevance and its freshest result was six weeks old, while these return today. The set is news engines plus Hacker News for the tech desk; qwant news earns its place by dating every result, which the others mostly do not and a story has to carry. Beware when editing: SearXNG does not error on an engine name it does not know -- it silently searches its default set, so a typo looks like a spectacularly good engine until you check which engine each result actually came from.

Reading a page, as distinct from finding one. A search returns a title, a URL and a snippet -- enough to know a story exists, not enough to report it, and certainly not enough to quote anybody. This lets a desk open the article it found. Registered separately from web_search on purpose: fetching an arbitrary URL the model chose is a wider door than querying one search host, so an operator can open the narrow one alone. The transport refuses anything that resolves off the public internet -- loopback, private ranges, and the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254 -- re-checked on every redirect, because a public host is free to redirect to 127.0.0.1. The url here is unused: the transport is chosen by the key.
